label: Lines and Cross-Ratios
notes: This chapter spans printed pages 67 through 78 and introduces the cross-ratio, the first genuinely projective number we meet. Frame it as the payoff of homogeneous coordinates: a quantity built from determinants that survives every projective map. Promise students that distance and ratio of distances will fail, but this ratio of ratios will not.

label: Joins and Meets by Cross Product
notes: Stress that the cross product is the single algebraic engine of the projective plane. The join of two points and the meet of two lines are the same operation, which is the cleanest expression of point-line duality. Have students notice that incidence reduces to a vanishing triple determinant, setting up the bracket algebra ahead.

label: Coordinates on a Projective Line
notes: Emphasize that a coordinate on a line is a chart choice, not the point itself. The pair lambda and mu is itself a point of the projective line RP one. Walk through how the affine value t equals lambda over mu loses exactly one point, the point at infinity, recovered by the reciprocal chart u equals one over t.

label: Defining the Cross-Ratio
notes: Define the cross-ratio carefully as a ratio of two ratios, then rewrite it with two by two brackets. Insist on the order of the four points, because permuting them changes the value. Point out that the bracket form needs no metric and no chart, only determinants of homogeneous representatives, which is why it generalizes the naive distance ratio.

label: Why Brackets Beat Distances
notes: Contrast the two formulas side by side. The signed length form is intuitive on a Euclidean line, but it breaks when a point goes to infinity. The bracket form computes straight through infinity and ignores how each representative is scaled. This robustness is the whole reason the cross-ratio, not the simple ratio, is the projective invariant.

label: Invariance Under Projective Maps
notes: Here is the central theorem. A two by two matrix acting on homogeneous coordinates multiplies every bracket by the same determinant of M. Because the cross-ratio is a quotient of products of brackets, that common factor cancels exactly. Walk the algebra slowly; the cancellation is the entire proof and students should see it line by line.

label: Perspectivities Preserve It
notes: Connect the algebra to geometry. Projecting four collinear points from a center onto a second line is a perspectivity, and chaining perspectivities gives projectivities. Each is realized by a projective matrix, so the cross-ratio is preserved. This is the result a Renaissance painter implicitly used and the reason photographs preserve cross-ratios of collinear features.

label: The Dual Cross-Ratio of Lines
notes: By duality the four concurrent lines through a point carry a cross-ratio equal to that of the four points they cut on any transversal. Explain that this is why a perspectivity preserves the value: the pencil of projecting lines has a fixed cross-ratio, and any line crossing the pencil reads off that same number.

label: The Harmonic Value -1
notes: Single out the value minus one as the most important special case. When the cross-ratio is minus one the pair C and D is harmonic with respect to A and B, and the relation is symmetric between the two pairs. Mention the midpoint and point at infinity example, since harmonicity quietly encodes the Euclidean midpoint inside projective language.

label: Constructing the Fourth Harmonic
notes: Walk the complete quadrilateral construction step by step. Given three collinear points, draw a quadrilateral whose diagonal structure meets the line again at the unique fourth harmonic point. Emphasize that this construction uses only a straightedge, needs no measurement, and yet pins down a point defined by the value minus one entirely projectively.

label: Six Values Under Permutation
notes: Explain that the cross-ratio depends on the order, but not arbitrarily. The twenty four permutations collapse to at most six values generated by lambda going to one over lambda and lambda going to one minus lambda. Show the orbit and note the degenerate coincidences at the harmonic value minus one, where the six values fall to three.

label: Recap and Outlook
notes: Recap the chain: joins and meets by cross product, coordinates on a line, the bracket definition, invariance by determinant cancellation, perspectivities, the harmonic case, and the six permutation values. Preview that the cross-ratio becomes the measuring tool for the rest of the book, underpinning Cayley-Klein distances and projective constructions of Euclidean structure.
